summary: Registers the H224 media type for the RTP payload format of H.224. In video conferencing, far-end camera control commonly uses ITU H.281 over H.224. The document also defines the SDP parameters needed. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: In a video call you can tilt or zoom the other person's camera. This gives the camera-control messages their official type name and call-setup settings.

questions: what is far end camera control
subtitle: Gives the far-end camera control messages used in video calls an official media type and SDP settings.

tldr.problem: Video conferencing systems let one side control the other side's camera, using H.281 over H.224. SDP-based systems had no registered media type to describe that channel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the media type application/h224 and defines how it maps to SDP: media name application, encoding name h224, clock rate 4800, plus offer/answer rules for the channel direction.
tldr.outcome: H.323 gateways and SDP-based systems can signal far-end camera control end to end without protocol translation in the middle.

today: RFC 4573 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4573 registers the H224 media type, which may be used by systems that use SDP (RFC 4566). The media type supports the simple far-end camera control protocol on SDP-based systems.

It helps signaling gateways between H.323 and SDP-based systems use far-end camera control end to end, without any protocol translation in the middle.
sections.plainLanguage: Some video systems speak one language and some speak another. A shared name for the camera remote control lets them understand each other.

sections.title: Far-End Camera Control Protocol
sections.content:
In conversational video, participants use a far-end camera control protocol (FECC) to control the remote camera. The protocol commonly used is ITU H.281 over H.224.

The protocol is based on ITU-T H.281 frames carried in ITU-T H.224 packets in an RTP/UDP channel. H.323 annex Q specifies how to build the RTP packets from the H.224 packets, and how to use the protocol in point-to-point and multipoint calls on packet-switch networks. FECC itself is internal to the H.224 frame and is identified by the client ID field of the H.224 packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The camera commands ride inside a small envelope, and that envelope travels inside the normal video-call traffic.

sections.title: Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers the MIME media type application/h224, using the templates from RFC 4288 and following RFC 3555. The type is application and the subtype is H224. There are no required parameters and no optional parameters.

The data is framed and binary. The intended usage is COMMON, and the applications that use it are video conferencing applications. Terminals sending simple far-end camera control commands should use this type, and receivers that cannot support the protocol will reject the channel.

The type depends on RTP framing, so it is only defined for transfer via RTP. Transport within other framing protocols is not defined. The change controller is the IETF Audio/Video Transport working group, delegated from the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like adding a new entry to an official list of file types, so everyone calls camera-control data by the same name.

sections.title: SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The media type maps to SDP fields as follows:

  • The media name in the m= line MUST be application. The transport SHALL be any applicable RTP profile, and the payload type is dynamic.
  • The encoding name in the a=rtpmap line MUST be h224.
  • The default clock rate in the a=rtpmap line MUST be 4800.

The recommended maximum bandwidth for this protocol is 6.4 kbit/sec.
sections.plainLanguage: When a call is set up, each side writes a short note saying what kind of data it will send. This part tells what to write for camera control.

sections.title: Use with the Offer/Answer Model
sections.content:
Camera control communication is uni-directional, but H.224 is bi-directional and can be used to learn the capabilities of the remote video endpoint, for example how many cameras it has. So the offer/answer exchange depends on what both sides can do.

The offerer offers a sendonly channel if its camera cannot be remotely controlled and it does not intend to use H.224 to learn the remote capabilities. Otherwise it offers sendrecv.

If the answerer gets sendonly, it answers recvonly if it supports far-end camera control, or ignores or rejects the offer. If it gets sendrecv and its camera can be remotely controlled, or it intends to use H.224 capabilities negotiation, it answers sendrecv. If its camera cannot be remotely controlled, it can answer sendonly. It may also reject the offer if it does not support FECC or does not intend to use it at the moment.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only want to steer the other camera, you say so. If you also let others steer yours, or want to ask what cameras they have, you say that instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
H.224 packets use the RTP header structure from RFC 3550, so they are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption, and SRTP (RFC 3711) may be used for both encryption and integrity protection.

A potential denial-of-service threat exists because data can cause application behavior such as camera movement. An attacker can inject pathological datagrams that make the receiver change the camera position. So data origin authentication and data integrity protection of at least the H.323 annex Q packet is RECOMMENDED, for example with SRTP. The right mechanism depends on the application, transport and signaling protocols, so other choices exist.
sections.plainLanguage: Without protection, a stranger could send fake commands and swing your camera around. Checking who sent each command stops that.
